discussion_comments.comment_body: Fixed in `d23386884`. The `afterRun` hook now awaits `next.afterRun(...)`, which resolves once the rule-based set is served. A one-shot run's `runtime.stop` therefore can no longer call `next.dispose` before the offer and debug-log entry are written, and the source, git and backlog read budgets bound the wait. The planner call and the connector refresh stay detached, and `plugin.test.ts` covers this by disposing right after `agent.run` while both are still pending.

Fixed in `d23386884`. `pruneSessionStates` still screens files with the async `stat`. For an expired file it now re-checks with `statSync` and removes it with `rmSync` with no await in between, so a state file rewritten while the first stat was pending is kept, as `session-state.test.ts` covers. A write from another process that lands between those two calls can still be lost, because there is no unlink-if-unchanged.

Fixed in `d11e7aca0`. `pruneSessionStates` now removes an expired file through `removeIfUnchanged`: it renames the file aside (atomic, so no write can interleave) and deletes it only if it is still the version whose age was checked (same inode, mtime and size); a version written since goes back with `linkSync`, which fails rather than overwrite a write that landed after the rename. `session-state.test.ts` covers a write after the last check and one that lands while a newer version is held aside.

Valid, and the window is wider than the comment says: `updateSessionStatus` in the persistence service retries a write whose status lock went stale, so when the two writes overlap the in-flight `running` fails its first attempt, re-reads the row and writes `running` on top of `cancelled`. The late writer always wins.

Fixed in "serialize session status writes so teardown's status lands last": status writes are chained per session on the same promise queue the compaction state already uses, so teardown's write waits for the in-flight one, and the shutting-down guard now runs when a write actually starts rather than when it is requested. The "drained prompt whose turn was still preparing" test now keeps the `running` write held across `stopSession` and asserts `cancelled` is not issued until it is released.

in practice, does this await take a while? I'm worried that a user will toggle the switch and the switch looks stuck for a second and the user tries switching back because they thinking something is broken

good call. I measured it in local runs..

An idle toggle flips in about 85ms, same as main. The switch only waits if you click it while a session is still being set up: right after another switch, right after sending a new task’s first message, or right after resuming a task from history. How long it waits is almost entirely the remote-config fetch every session start does:
- fast API: a rebuild takes about 300ms
- API delayed 1.5s: about 1.8s
- API unresponsive: the fetch waits out its 10s timeout, so a rebuild takes about 10.3s, and a toggle landing mid-rebuild sat unflipped for 6.3s in my run

I tried to play with other factors (repo size, a hundred rules, skills and workflows, long transcripts and MCP), and they barely moved it.

For comparison, those same three moments are exactly when main breaks. The switch flips instantly, but the session ends up in the other mode. A slow API makes that more likely in exactly the cases where this PR waits longer.

So **yes, the “stuck” switch is real on slow networks**. But I think the inconsistent state is the bigger problem. It’s silent, it doesn’t heal on its own (toggling back and forth didn’t help the reporter), and it costs the user real work. The stuck switch is visible, ends on its own, and is safe: clicking again just asks for the same mode, and anything sent meanwhile waits and runs in the mode you end up seeing.

For the toggle itself, we could do this as a follow-up:
1. Flip the switch immediately with a pending state (dimmed slider or a “Switching to Act…” tooltip), and flip it back with a short explanation if the switch fails. Maybe a notification only if the wait gets long, so it doesn’t nag on every slow toggle
2. Coalesce rapid toggles, so Plan then Act before the first rebuild starts only rebuilds once

Implemented in `84db143`.

The response is claimed before the first asynchronous delivery step, so a second submission cannot resolve the same question. It is routed through the normal follow-up path while the claimed response continues delivering its attachments. I kept the session identity check and retained a per-attempt validity token so cancellation, replacement questions, delivery failures, and retries remain safe: an old callback cannot become current again after a retry, and a failed attempt releases only its own claim.

The focused VS Code suites cover the overlap, cancellation, failure/retry, and stale-callback cases and pass; SDK typecheck also passes. The separate display fix keeps the original pending-question text in the submitted event while preserving the expanded model prompt.

🟡 **bug** (medium)

The `findLastIndex(..., m => m.say === "checkpoint_created")` lookup now runs inside the background promise (after `commit()` resolves) instead of while this call is still the newest checkpoint. Since commits are no longer awaited, two `saveCheckpoint()` calls can overlap — the agent routinely runs several tools back to back, and the comment you added notes a commit can take seconds on large shadow git repos. When the earlier commit resolves, this lookup finds the *newest* `checkpoint_created` message and writes its hash there, so the message that actually belongs to that commit stays without a `lastCheckpointHash`; if the commits resolve out of order, a message can even end up carrying a different checkpoint's hash. Both cases corrupt the per-message hash that 'Restore checkpoint' and `doesLatestTaskCompletionHaveNewChanges()` rely on.

**建议**: Resolve the target message synchronously instead of by re-searching later: right after `await this.say("checkpoint_created")` capture the message index/`ts` of the message you just created, and inside the `.then()` callback update exactly that captured message (re-validate it still exists). Alternatively serialize commits by chaining/storing the in-flight promise.

discussion_comments.comment_body: Fixed. The record is now forgotten only when `CloudSessionHost.whenTurnAccepted()` resolves, i.e. when the Hub reports run activity for the session or `runTurn` returns, not when the send is launched. If a host exits after acceptance but before forgetting, recovery inspects the sandbox and leaves it if it has taken a turn. Covered by `keeps a provisioning sandbox recorded until the sandbox accepts its first turn`.

[P2] Prevent a retired pane's failed send from overwriting the current draft

`setPromptInput` now writes this app-owned Map, but `ChatThreadPane.handleSend` still decides whether to restore a failed prompt using its own `promptInputRef` after `await sendPrompt` (page.tsx:1915–1923). Send in A with a slow session start/reattach, navigate to B and back to A, and type a newer draft before the original start fails. The old pane's ref is still empty, so its continuation writes the submitted prompt over the new pane's cached draft. The visible input still contains the newer text, but another navigation restores the old submitted text and loses the newer draft.

I reproduced this with the real `usePromptDraft` and a deferred rejection through the real `useChatSession`; I also executed the production `handleSend` extracted from page.tsx. Validate the current draft revision/thread lifetime before restoring, rather than relying on a retired instance's ref. Add a deferred-send regression across A → B → A and another remount; the newer draft must survive. The same guard should keep late recovery from reinserting a draft after its thread was deleted and pruned.

Good catch, fixed in 98d674cfa. shutdownSession now deletes the slot only when it still points at the runtime being shut down, the same guard releaseSessionRuntime already had. Regression test: a stop stalled in the resident's agent shutdown while a same-id start registers the replacement; the replacement stays reachable afterwards (fails with session_not_found without the guard).

`waitUntilSettled` has no production caller left — this PR removes the one that existed (`await this.sessionRebuilds.waitUntilSettled()` in `SdkController`), and the send path now goes through `handlePendingRebuilds`, which parks the follow-up and returns `"deferred"` rather than awaiting. Only the scheduler's own tests reference it now. Worth dropping unless a caller is coming: a test-only affordance on a production class tends to acquire one later without the concurrency implications getting re-examined.

Dropped in b3cb45d, along with `hasPendingRebuild` and the settled-waiter list. The follow-up path no longer awaits the scheduler at all; a running-turn follow-up goes straight to Core's queue and the rebuild waits for the queue to drain.
